## Setting and question

In 2014 the Affordable Care Act offered states the option of expanding Medicaid to adults
under 138% of the federal poverty line, and opened the Marketplace for subsidised private
insurance. Medicaid spending rose in expansion states with the new enrollment.

Whether it displaced spending by other payers is less understood. If expansion moved
people out of private plans, or shifted the cost of care they already received, private
and Medicare spending should fall in expansion states relative to states that did not
expand. We test that hypothesis on coverage, spending and encounters for all three
payers.

## Data and design

IHME Disease Expenditure Project (DEX 2.0): state-level spending and encounters by payer
and setting, all ages, 2010--2018, fit to SHEA state expenditure.
Uninsurance from CPS. **25 states** expanded on 1 January 2014;
the **19** that never expanded serve as controls. Later expanding
cohorts are dropped (n ≤ 3 per year).

Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) group-time difference-in-differences against the
never-expanded states, conditioning on covariates $X$: poverty rate, median household
income, pre-expansion uninsurance, and the shares under 18 and over 65:

```{=typst}
#block(width: 100%, above: 6mm, below: 6mm)[#set text(size: 26pt)
$ Delta Y_t = Y_t - Y_2013 $
$ "ATT"(t) = bb(E) [Delta Y_t | D=1] - bb(E) [bb(E) [Delta Y_t | X, D=0] | D=1] $]
```

Figures plot $\mathrm{ATT}(t)$; tables report its 2014--2018 average. **Inference** is a
multiplier bootstrap, 1,000 draws, clustered on state. **Parallel trends** is a Wald test
of $\mathrm{ATT}(t)=0$ across the three pre-expansion placebo years, $\chi^2_3$ on the
analytic clustered variance. **Multiplicity** is Benjamini--Hochberg across the 66
estimates in panel 4.

## 1. Expansion covered the uninsured

```{=typst}
#align(center, image("figures/f1_coverage.png", width: 82%))
```

| Coverage | Effect | 95% CI | Pre-test |
|:---------|-------:|:-------|---------:|
| Medicaid  | +3.69 | [+2.27, +5.12] | 0.84 |
| Medicare  | −0.20 | [−0.54, +0.14] | 0.72 |
| Uninsured | −1.38 | [−2.48, −0.28] | 0.30 |
| Private   | −2.16 | [−3.07, −1.24] | 0.96 |

Medicaid coverage rose **3.7 points** more in expansion states, and the uninsured rate
fell a further **1.4 points**. Private coverage grew in both groups, 62.9 to 64.4% in
expanders and 62.6 to 66.5% in controls, so **−2.2** is controls gaining faster, not
expanders losing: Marketplace subsidies reach 100 to 138% FPL where Medicaid does not.

```{=typst}
#colbreak()
```
### 2. New Medicaid enrollees had similar healthcare consumption

![](figures/f2_medicaid.png)

```{=typst}
#note[Difference-in-differences effect at each year relative to 2014, as a percentage of the pre-expansion level in expansion states. 95% intervals from multiplier bootstrap.]
```

Spending across expansion states rose **18.0%** (SE 3.9) after expansion alongside **19.9%**
increased enrollment, an additional **$189 per resident per year** on a pre-expansion base
of $1,051. Spending per enrollee was not affected: **−3.3%** (SE 4.4), so the states that
expanded bought more of the same care rather than more expensive care.

### 3. No decline in private spending

![](figures/f3_private.png)

Private spending per enrollee follows an increasing but insignificant path across
2014--2018, averaging **+4.8%** (SE 2.8) above the pre-expansion level; per resident the
average is **+1.7%** (SE 2.4). Neither margin shows the reduction that crowd-out would
produce.

Encounters per enrollee are positive in all five settings, **+2.2 to +5.5%**, and
significant in none, so what movement there is looks like use rather than price.

The interval on spending per resident, **[−3.0, +6.3]%**, excludes a fall larger than 3%
of the pre-expansion level, or about **$80 per resident per year**. That is the tightest
bound the design supports against crowd-out.

```{=typst}
#colbreak()
```
## 4. No effect outside Medicaid

We find no significant effect of the 2014 expansion on spending or encounters, per
resident or per enrollee, in any setting, for any payer other than Medicaid. Of the **66
estimates** below, four survive correction for multiple comparisons, and all four are
Medicaid on the per-resident margin. Among the **44 non-Medicaid** estimates, one clears
5% before correction and none survives it.

Precision is uneven. On the aggregate margins the intervals bound the effect: Medicare
spending per resident is **+0.4%** [−2.3, +3.0] and private **+1.7%** [−3.0, +6.3],
ruling out displacement larger than 3% of either payer's pre-expansion spending. In the
nursing and pharmacy cells they span 14 to 21 points, where the statement is insufficient
evidence rather than no effect.

## Limitations

Estimates apply to the 2014 cohort and the never-expanded states; the seven later
expanding cohorts are excluded because at one to three states each, the estimator's
variance is not identified.

**Out-of-pocket spending is excluded.** DEX combines cost-sharing by the insured with all
spending by the uninsured, and expansion moves that mix.

Coverage is a state-level share, so we see that private coverage grew more slowly in
expansion states, not which individuals switched.

**Null results are bounded, not confirmed.** We report intervals rather than equivalence
tests, so the claim is that effects larger than those bounds are excluded.
